title: The road houses
hookLine: caravanserais on trade routes, where travelers stayed

lines: TRAVEL IS A PIECE OF TORMENT.
cards: A saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, in Sahih al-Bukhari, is startlingly honest: travel is a piece of torment.
It keeps you from your sleep, your food and your drink, so when you've finished what you went for, hurry home to your family. Anyone who has slept on an airport floor knows.

The old trade roads were harder: dust by day, cold at night, thieves in the hills. Along them, people built houses for exactly that torment. You met the Seljuk ones in Anatolia; this time, the idea underneath them all.

teach.h: THE LAW MAKES ROOM FOR THE ROAD.
teach.b: Start with how the faith treats the traveler, because the stone follows from it. The Qur'an makes room for someone on the road.
A person on a journey in Ramadan may leave the fast and make up the days later, it says in surah two. And prayer may be shortened.
In Pickthall's translation: "And when ye go forth in the land, it is no sin for you to curtail (your) worship." The verse goes on to name the fear of attack.
In Sahih Muslim, someone later asks Umar why people still shorten, now that the roads are safe. Umar says he wondered the same and asked the Prophet, who called it a charity from God, to be accepted.

teach.h: IBN AL-SABIL, SON OF THE ROAD.
teach.b: The Qur'an also names ibn al-sabil, the son of the road, the wayfarer, among those owed a share of charity. So the law leans toward the tired, and the road house leans the same way.
Out on the open road it was called a caravanserai; inside a city, often a khan.
Most share a pattern: one great gate shut at night, a courtyard open to the sky, a well or fountain, rooms around the edge for people, stalls or arcades for the animals, often a small mosque.
In cities the khan was also a warehouse and market, where far-off merchants stored bales and struck deals. On the road it was shelter, and in some, paid for by waqf, the night cost nothing.
A road house turns a stranger into a guest for a night. But the honest hadith still holds: a road house isn't home. It's a place to gather strength to keep going, or to go back.

how: Muslim travelers shorten their prayers on journeys and may postpone a Ramadan fast; zakat and other charity can go to the wayfarer, and restored caravanserais and khans still stand in cities and along old routes in Turkey, Iran and the Arab world.

o: a road house where travelers and their animals rested
a long line of camels and traders crossing a desert
a covered market where merchants sold silk and spice

p: the wayfarer, the son of the road
a road house in a city, with a market

s: the Qur'an asks travelers to keep every rule exactly as at home
it lets travelers shorten prayer and make up a missed Ramadan fast later.

games.q: you're on a long, hard journey during Ramadan. what does the Qur'an allow?
o: you must fast every day no matter what.
you may leave the fast now and make up the days later.
travelers never have to make up the fast.
games.why: surah two lets someone on a journey make up the days later, and 4:101, with the Prophet's answer in Sahih Muslim, lets prayer be shortened on the road. the law leans toward the tired.

practice: Think of someone on the road today, a friend flying, a cousin driving through the night, a stranger asking directions, and decide one real help: a message, a meal, a ride, a little patience.
If you pray, you can ask for their safe return.

wordCard.voice: Caravanserai. A road house with a gate, a well and a room, so a stranger could rest as a guest. Today's word.
